title: Efficient permuted intron-exon RNA circularization system based on the LtrB group II Intron from Lactococcus lactis
authors: Castillo, K. D.; Seephetdee, C.; Horikawa, W.; Kiss, D. L.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as promising platforms for stable RNA expression and therapeutic applications, but methods for their generation remain limited. Here, we engineered the Lactococcus lactis LtrB group II intron into a permuted intron-exon (PIE) configuration to enable efficient circRNA formation (circLtrB). Among the tested split designs, LtrB domain IV cleavage yielded the highest circularization efficiency. Although LtrB encodes LtrA maturase required for efficient in vivo splicing, in vitro application of LtrA to the PIE constructs resulted in lower circularization efficiency than self-splicing conditions. We further examined circularization under distinct salt conditions and showed that NH4Cl- and KCl-based splicing buffers independently support high circularization efficiencies (>80%), while producing distinct splicing intermediates, indicating ion-specific mechanistic effects on circularization. Extending outer homology arms did not enhance circularization efficiency, demonstrating that efficient circRNA formation in the circLtrB platform is independent of extended exon pairing interactions. Using this system, we generated circRNAs across a range of coding sequence lengths, highlighting its payload flexibility. To optimize translation, we evaluated multiple internal ribosome entry sites (IRES), including Aichivirus, Crohivirus, CVB3, improved EMCV, HRV, and Salivirus, and found that the CVB3 IRES drove the highest translation efficiency. Linear NLuc showed faster decay kinetics, while circLtrB-NLuc exhibited more sustained expression over time. Transcriptome-wide RNA sequencing revealed comparable innate immune responses between circular and linear RNAs. Together, these results establish circLtrB as a versatile and efficient platform for circRNA production, providing mechanistic insight into group II intron-mediated circularization and expanding the toolkit for functional circRNA engineering.

title: A Plasmodium falciparum Pangenome Resource to Drive Structural Variant Discovery and to assist Malaria Control
authors: Billows, N.; Thorpe, J.; Campino, S.; Clark, T. G.
abstract: Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest causative agent of malaria, harbours extensive structural variation that underlies key biological processes including drug resistance and diagnostic evasion. Here, we present PfPan, a P. falciparum pangenome constructed from 13 geographically diverse high-quality reference genomes using Minigraph-Cactus, adding 4.77 Mb of sequence beyond the 3D7 linear reference. We identify over 5,000 structural variants (SVs) across the reference genomes and demonstrate improved genotyping using the vg toolkit compared to linear reference-based approaches, with comparable performance for small variant discovery. Benchmarking against assembly-derived truth sets confirms pangenome superiority for structural variant detection, particularly at complex and hypervariable loci. Applying PfPan to 878 globally sampled P. falciparum whole-genome sequences, we characterise biologically and clinically relevant SVs, including the complex drug resistance-linked gch1 locus, and explore deletions upstream of the coding sequence for the diagnostic target HRP2. PfPan provides a foundational resource for mitigating reference bias in P. falciparum genomic surveillance and establishes a framework for improved detection of variants associated with drug resistance and malaria control in monoclonal P. falciparum samples that have not undergone selective whole-genome amplification.

title: Partial lesions of hypocretin neurons of the rat lateral hypothalamus affect wake and sleep regulation under increased sleep pressure
authors: Lebedeva, M.; Levcik, D.; Kudlacek, J.; Maleninska, K.; Vojtechova, I.; Buchtova, H.; Brozka, H.; Radostova, D.; Petranova, E.; Jiruska, P.; Svoboda, J.; Kubik, S.; Kelemen, E.; Stuchlik, A.
abstract: Hypocretin(orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamic area are important for sleep and wake regulation in mammals and their damage in humans manifests clinically as narcolepsy. While in previous studies experimentally induced massive loss of these neurons revealed their physiological importance, small lesions and their manifestations can uncover more subtle features of sleep regulation and help understand the delicate processes in early stages of pathogenesis of narcolepsy. We studied the effects of partial lesions (approximately 30%) of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus on sleep patterns and EEG in rats. The lesions did not change the normal sleep and wake pattern in undisturbed rats. The effects of lesions manifested under increased sleep pressure after six hours of sleep deprivation, when they led to accelerated dynamics of compensatory slow wave sleep. The lesions also led to a slight decrease in theta frequency in wakefulness and in REM sleep, which we observed during undisturbed sleep and wake behavior as well as after sleep deprivation.

title: Artificial hibernation uncovers distinct interaction dynamics in functional and pathological state change
authors: Mercier, D.; Chiang, M.-C.; Saito, V. M.; Lin, Y.-J.; Ashitomi, H.; Oshiro, M.; Takahashi-Nakazato, A.; Tanaka, K. Z.
abstract: Neural population activity can reorganize without disrupting function, but how such changes differ from those associated with pathology remains unknown. Artificial hibernation, Q-neuron-induced hypothermia and hypometabolism (QIH), causes extensive synaptic remodeling in the hippocampus without erasing established memories, allowing us to examine how extensive network reorganization can occur without lasting functional impairment. Longitudinal calcium imaging showed that hippocampal activity recovered after QIH without returning to its pre-hibernation population configuration. Instead, QIH reorganized neuronal activity patterns and coactivity beyond representational drift. Electrophysiological recordings revealed that this reorganization of neuronal interactions depended on the preceding network state. In mice subjected to kainic acid-induced status epilepticus, QIH reduced seizure-associated increases in neuronal interactions and spike coactivity during sharp-wave ripples. Over the following 50 days, the divergence of hippocampal LFP trajectories was constrained, and the progressive development of electrophysiological and histological pathology was attenuated. These findings suggest that controlled, extensive reorganization of neural population activity can prevent the progression toward pathological network states, with changes in neuronal interactions, particularly sharp-wave ripple-associated coactivity, accompanying this process.

title: Disentangling evoked and induced activity from single-trial neurophysiological time series
authors: Ahola, O.; Haxel, L.; Ziemann, U.; Ilmoniemi, R.; Lioumis, P.
abstract: Evoked and induced responses are fundamental neurophysiological readouts in the development and assessment of treatments for disorders with impaired neural function. Distinguishing these responses is essential for interpreting single-trial variability, identifying the determinants of these responses, and enabling real-time probing of cortical responsiveness. However, because of dynamic overlap, separating evoked and induced activity remains unsolved at the single-trial level when instantaneous fluctuations of cortical responsiveness are of interest. We developed the Evoked-Ongoing/Induced Separator (EOIS), a framework for separating event-evoked, ongoing, and event-modulated induced activity from single-trial data. EOIS recovers evoked and ongoing/induced components by leveraging their distinct phase-consistency features in MEG and real-time EEG, enabling subject-agnostic single-trial time-series analysis and attribution of cortical response variability to specific components. By delivering component-resolved time series, EOIS enables biomarker refinement, pharmacodynamic readouts, and closed-loop neuromodulation, facilitating translational deployment across individuals and care settings.

title: Predicting alcohol consumption from resting-state functional connectivity: Feature relevance and the potential of meta-matching.
authors: Bottino, M.; Smolka, M. N.; Böhmer, J.; Yeo, T. B. T.; Bach, P.; Kiefer, F.; Lenz, B.; Heinz, A.; Spitta, G.; Rosenthal, A.; Ritter, K.; Rane, R. P.; Garg, S.; Schwarz, E.; ReCoDe Consortium,  ; Walter, H.; Marxen, M.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is among the most prevalent mental disorders. Associations between resting-state fMRI functional connectivity (FC) and AUD have been reported but rarely replicated. In this preregistered study, we investigated the extent to which FC predicts alcohol consumption, as measured by the AUDIT-C score, in a large sample of non-treatment-seeking alcohol consumers (N = 739), including 528 participants with varying degrees of AUD severity. To optimize performance, we compared kernel ridge regression (KRR) trained directly on this sample with transfer-learning models based on multilayer meta-matching embeddings, from which we derived data-driven relevance maps at the connection, region, and network levels. We tested split-half reliability, reproducibility across cohorts, and outcome specificity of the relevance maps. Both models predicted AUDIT-C scores moderately but significantly (r {approx} 0.15). Meta-matching did not outperform KRR in prediction. Relevance maps showed limited split-half reliability, consistent with the modest predictive performance, but reproduced moderately well across two independent cohorts. These maps indicate reduced connectivity among limbic regions, the anterior middle temporal gyrus, the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal attention network regions. In contrast, hypothesized hyperconnectivity patterns involving the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus were less reliable and mostly non-significant. Overall, our findings suggest that resting-state FC contains reproducible but weak signals related to alcohol consumption. Transfer learning improved relevance-map reliability but not prediction performance and reduced outcome specificity. These results support the utility of interpretable machine learning for identifying connectivity patterns related to drinking behavior, while also highlighting current limitations in its predictive power.

title: Open-source virtual reality platform for head-fixed adult zebrafish
authors: Javier, A.; Narayanan, S.; Anneser, L.; van Krugten, J.; Friedrich, R. W.
abstract: Virtual realities (VRs) are powerful tools to study how brains interact with the world through behavior. We present a new platform for closed-loop high-resolution virtual-reality experiments in head-fixed adult zebrafish. The VR is defined using open-source software, projected onto a semi-hexagonal tank by three projectors, and controlled by software allowing for modular trial-and-block experimental designs. Real time VR updates are performed by an optimized algorithm based on infrared tail videos. Two-photon imaging during behavior is achieved by custom gating of VR projectors and coordinated with stimulus triggers by a microcontroller. Using this system we found that fish respond to visual landmarks in virtual corridors with distinct changes in locomotion parameters and body posture. Adding landmarks to a familiar corridor elicited localized behavioral responses that decayed with experience. Restricting the viewing distance by simulating 'murky water' further confirmed that behavioral responses were driven by the visibility of landmarks independent of their position. Our platform provides a user-friendly, versatile VR system for the joint analysis of neuronal activity and behavior in adult zebrafish

title: Alpha-synuclein and neuromelanin converge to promote Parkinsons disease pathology
authors: Nicolau-Vera, A.; Gonzalez-Sepulveda, M.; Cladera-Sastre, J. M.; Cuadros, T.; Parent, A.; Roch, G.; Marongiu, J.; Huynh, B.; Mahabadian, A. A.; Su, F.; Chatterton, Z.; Hoyo, J.; Laguna, A.; Fu, Y.; Halliday, G.; Vila, M.
abstract: Parkinsons disease (PD) is defined by the preferential degeneration of neuromelanin (NM)-containing dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra (SN), accompanied by intraneuronal inclusions rich in alpha-synuclein (aSYN). However, the mechanistic relationship between NM accumulation and aSYN pathology remains unclear. Here, we reveal a bidirectional pathogenic relationship between aSYN and NM. In human post-mortem midbrain tissue, ventral nigral neurons with high NM content display increased aSYN mRNA expression and are preferentially lost in PD. In a rat model that recapitulates age-dependent, human-like NM accumulation via targeted tyrosinase (TYR) expression, co-expression of aSYN accelerates NM buildup, enhances aSYN oligomerization, and aggravates nigrostriatal degeneration. Mechanistically, aSYN oligomerization in NM-producing rats decreases vesicular dopamine storage and impairs vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane, increasing cytosolic dopamine availability for oxidation into NM. Together, these findings support a pathogenic feedback loop in which elevated aSYN accelerates NM synthesis through disrupted dopamine compartmentalization, while NM accumulation further promotes aSYN aggregation and neuronal loss. This aSYN-NM axis may underlie the preferential vulnerability of pigmented nigral neurons in PD and provide a mechanistic framework for the development of future targeted therapeutics.

title: Transiently-elevated dopamine triggers plasticity that preserves motor function, striatal neuron morphology, and thalamostriatal input in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease
authors: Brague, J. C.; Sinha, G. P.; Henry, D. A.; Headrick, D. J.; Hooks, B. M.; Seal, R. P.
abstract: Loss of nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neurons in Parkinson's disease (PD) produces motor symptoms by disrupting the normal circuitry of striatal projection neurons. Here, we report that the Transient Elevation of Dopamine (TED) within a defined window of 6-OHDA-induced DA depletion preserves normal motor behaviorfor months. We also observed a preservation of mature spines specifically on direct pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs) and not indirect pathway striatal projection neurons (iSPNs). Preservation of motor behavior and dSPN spines required enhanced activation of striatal D1 receptors. Circuit mapping showed input from primary motor cortex was reduced, while input from parafascicular thalamus was unchanged in both TED mice and controls of both sexes, suggesting rewiring of excitatory inputs to dSPNs from other cortical or thalamic areas in TED mice. Lastly, thalamostriatal paired pulse facilitation, normally depressed following DA depletion, is preserved in TED mice. Although the causal basis of motor preservation remains unresolved, our findings reveal that a schedule of transiently increasing striatal DA surrounding the depletion of dopamine can engage a long-lasting plasticity that markedly delays the onset of motor impairment

title: Semaglutide Increases Striatal Leptin Sensitivity, Impacting Dopaminergic Response to Cocaine
authors: Muldowney, J. J.; Umlauf, M. C.; Bocarsly, M. E.
abstract: There is accumulating evidence that the GLP-1 analog, semaglutide, might effectively curb intake of cocaine via brain dopaminergic functioning, despite limited brain penetrance. However, there is currently no established mechanism elucidating how chronic semaglutide treatment regulates the dopaminergic response to cocaine. Cocaine is a highly addictive substance that produces rewarding effects primarily through antagonism of the dopamine transporter (DAT). Therapeutics for cocaine use disorder (CUD) have long targeted DAT in the hope of reducing cocaine intake. Metabolic hormones such as leptin and insulin have been shown to influence DAT, and for that reason have been explored for the regulation of cocaine reward and behavior. Interestingly, while semaglutide does not penetrate the brain, it does peripherally modulate metabolic hormones that enter the brain. Through fast-scan cyclic voltammetry and behavioral experimentation, we examined the effects of chronic semaglutide treatment on dopamine signaling, cocaine-induced dopamine release, and locomotor sensitivity. We determined that chronic semaglutide inhibits dopaminergic reward induced by cocaine. Surprisingly, semaglutides effects on cocaine reward were blunted in mice fasted overnight, suggesting a mechanistic dependence on metabolic hormones. Semaglutide administration generated significant reductions in fasting blood leptin, as well as enhanced striatal leptin sensitivity compared to vehicle controls. Preceding cocaine exposure, application of leptin to fasted mice restored semaglutides regulation of cocaine. Our results exhibit a potential mechanism for semaglutide-induced cocaine reward inhibition, emphasizing the potential of central leptin signaling as a therapeutic target for CUD.

title: Classic and novel features of the dentate gyrus vascular niche quantified through 3D vessel reconstruction
authors: Carter, I.; Smith, B. M.; Kirby, E. D.
abstract: Adult neurogenesis, the continued generation of new neurons throughout life, supports a variety of emotional and cognitive functions in mammals. Lifelong neurogenesis occurs in the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus, where a neurogenic niche supports the survival and growth of neural stem cells (NSCs), which divide to generate new neurons. A key component of this niche is the surrounding vasculature, thought to give NSCs access to circulating support molecules, oxygen, and nutrient metabolites. The DG vasculature is strikingly variable across layers. Vascular density and linearity, for example, have been noted to differ substantially in the different cell layers that make up the DG. Most of these prior descriptions of the DG vasculature have been qualitative, and other important aspects of vessel morphology, like vessel diameter, have not been previously reported to our knowledge. To provide a more complete and quantitative description of the adult DG vasculature, we used a 3D imaging technique to fully characterize the vasculature of each DG cellular layer. Our 3D reconstructions of DG blood vessels provide a quantitative method for measuring several known, qualitative features of the neurogenic niche, such as blood vessel density and tortuosity. In some cases, we reproduce qualitative observations, such as affirming that vessel density is high in the subgranular zone (SGZ) where NSCs reside and low in the granule cell layer. In other cases, our findings go counter to what qualitative observations suggest. For example, the SGZ is often described as having uniquely linear blood vessels, but we found that linearity was similar between the SGZ and hilus layer. We also report new measures of features of DG layer vascular architecture: vessel diameter and branching. Together, these findings offer a global, quantitative characterization of the DG vascular niche in adult mice. Beyond providing more detailed characterization of DG vasculature, we also anticipate our methods and estimates of variance in mice will be useful for investigators wishing to plan their own quantitative studies of changes in the vascular structure of the DG.

title: Nanoscale remodeling of synaptic glutamate receptors and calcium channels in temporal lobe epilepsy
authors: Kaufmann, W. A.; Venturino, A.; Kleindienst, D.; Roessler, K.; Czech, T.; Janssen, J. M.; Engelhardt, M.; Stefanits, H.; Watanabe, M.; Siegert, S.; Shigemoto, R.
abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most common form of focal epilepsy and remains drug-resistant in approximately one-third of patients, for whom surgical resection of the epileptogenic zone is currently the most effective treatment option. One strategy to improve therapeutic outcomes involves identifying the molecular mechanisms and key regulators underlying synaptic function. Although altered glutamatergic neurotransmission is considered a major contributor to epileptic hyperexcitability, the nanoscale organization of key synaptic proteins in the human epileptic cortex is still not well characterized. In particular, it remains unclear whether pre- and postsynaptic proteins undergo synapse-type-specific remodeling in TLE. Here, we used high-resolution freeze-fracture replica immunolabeling to map the nanoscale organization of postsynaptic AMPA receptors (AMPARs) and presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2.1) in glutamatergic synapses of cortical layers II/III of surgically resected human tissue. We examined perilesional, cytologically unremarkable, non-epileptogenic cortical tissue obtained from patients undergoing tumor resection (52-63 years; two female and three male patients) and compared these data with cortical samples from patients with refractory TLE (22-53 years; two female and four male patients). To assess whether pathological remodeling differs across synapse populations, we analyzed both excitatory dendritic spine and shaft synapses. We found a robust, highly consistent increase in AMPAR density at both spine and shaft synapses in TLE patients indicating enhanced postsynaptic excitatory signaling. However, AMPAR spatial reorganization differed between synapse types. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated that spine synapses largely preserved a random receptor distribution without a significant clustering pattern, whereas shaft synapses exhibited a redistribution from clustering toward random receptor arrangements together with reduced center-preference within the postsynaptic density. In contrast, presynaptic CaV2.1 remodeling was more variable and predominantly associated with excitatory spine synapses. TLE spine synapses exhibited an overall increase in CaV2.1 density together with significantly larger and more numerous CaV2.1 nanoclusters within the active zone. This difference was particularly pronounced in male patients. In comparison, shaft synapses displayed only minor presynaptic alterations. CaV2.1 channels remained highly clustered under both control and epileptic conditions, indicating preservation of core active-zone organizational features despite disease-associated nanoscale remodeling. Together, these findings provide direct ultrastructural support that pathological plasticity in human TLE involves an overall increase in excitatory postsynaptic responsiveness and a target cell-specific increase of excitatory release probability at cortical synapses.

title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult Xenopus laevis
authors: Murugan, N. J.; Russell, S.; Kaplan, D.; Levin, M.; Miller, K.
abstract: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24 hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post-treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. We detected no corresponding increase in brain ISR score. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression, and increased gdf15.L. Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction and identify candidate mechanisms of brain body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.

title: Muscarinic signaling sustains delay-period selectivity in prefrontal cortex by preserving thalamic drive
authors: Kim, Y.; Kim, J.; Choi, I. S.; Lee, J.; Yang, Y.-S.; Choi, J. H.; Choi, J.-W.; Rah, J.-C.
abstract: Short-term memory (STM) requires the temporary maintenance of task-relevant information in prefrontal cortex (PFC). Reciprocal interactions between the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) and PFC have been implicated in sustaining this activity, but how thalamofrontal communication is maintained despite the biophysical constraints of repetitive synaptic transmission remains unclear. Here, we show that MD--PFC synapses exhibit profound frequency-dependent short-term depression, causing repetitive thalamic input to progressively lose its ability to drive PFC neurons. During STM performance, acetylcholine (ACh) levels in PFC rose rapidly following cue presentation and remained elevated throughout the delay period. Muscarinic ACh receptor (mAChR) activation did not alleviate synaptic depression, but instead increased the intrinsic excitability of PFC neurons, thereby preserving their responsiveness to weakened thalamic input. Conversely, mAChR blockade impaired STM performance and progressively disrupted delay-period directional representations at both the single-neuron and population levels, while largely sparing initial encoding. These findings identify muscarinic signaling as a postsynaptic gain mechanism that compensates for declining thalamofrontal efficacy and sustains task-relevant prefrontal representations during STM.

title: Engineered proteins to restore and enhance neurotransmitter release
authors: Chin, M.; Yang, K.; Lopez, R. C.; Tan, C.; Kaeser, P. S.
abstract: Synapse dysfunction is a hallmark feature of many neurological diseases. Synaptic transmission is initiated in nerve terminals, where active zone protein complexes control vesicle fusion for neurotransmitter release. Here, we engineer proteins that mediate active zone functions and demonstrate their use for reconstituting and strengthening neurotransmission. A protein composed of CaV{beta}4 and the RIM1 zinc finger, {beta}4-Zn, restored neurotransmitter release after active zone disruption through recruitment of Munc13. We develop {beta}4-MC, derived from the Munc13-1 MUN and C2C domains, which bypasses Munc13 recruitment and directly mediates vesicle docking, priming and fusion after active zone disruption. In {beta}4-MC, MUN domain functions are dispensable for docking, but active MUN and C2C domains are both necessary for neurotransmitter release. In wild-type mouse and human neurons, {beta}4-MC but not {beta}4-Zn strengthens neurotransmitter release. Furthermore, {beta}4-Zn and {beta}4-MC restore and enhance dopamine release in the mouse striatum, respectively. Hence, {beta}4 proteins are engineered secretory proteins with therapeutic potential as enhancers of synaptic function.

title: A genome-wide catalog of sites where peripheral DNA methylation reflects the brain
authors: Nishitani, S.; Han, S.; Ishii, T.; Shimura, A.; Phuong, N. J.; Kato, A.; Chambers, M.; Wang, T.; Isozaki, M.; Higashino, Y.; Yamauchi, T.; Kawajiri, S.; Arishima, H.; Kodera, T.; Imoto, H.; Nomura, S.; Yamanishi, K.; Aoyama, B.; Genc, I.; Sakuma, R.; Nguyen, H. D.; Gorantla, N.; Ghasemi, E.; Yao, A.; Kurata, S.; Fujisawa, T. X.; Braun, P. R.; Nagao, T.; Yamanashi, T.; Tomoda, A.; Kikuta, K.; Ooka, T.; Grant, G. A.; Hooper, J. E.; Howard, M. A.; Kawasaki, H.; Potash, J. B.; Snyder, M. P.; Shinozaki, G.
abstract: Epigenetic studies of psychiatric and neurological disorders rely largely on peripheral tissues, yet where peripheral DNA methylation (DNAm) reflects the brain remains unclear. We generated a paired brain and peripheral DNAm dataset from 148 donors in three cohorts and combined it with five published cohorts for consensus brain-peripheral correlations. By cross-validation across cohorts, we defined brain epigenome shared sites (BrESS), more than 100,000 CpGs per tissue at which peripheral DNAm reproducibly predicts brain DNAm. BrESS lay at promoters active in both brain and periphery and in housekeeping genes, and most were not explained by genetic effects. BrESS did not contribute to the heritability of seven disorders, and CpGs from epigenome-wide association studies of these disorders were not enriched at BrESS. Peripheral DNAm reflects the brain mainly in a regulatory compartment shared across tissues, outside which disease signals largely lie, and BrESS separate peripheral signals attributable to the brain from others.

title: Sound-Driven Motion of Human Cochlear Structures Depends on Organ of Corti Integrity
authors: Secchia, P.; McHugh, C. I.; Cho, N. H.; Zosuls, A.; Tubelli, A.; Puria, S.; Nakajima, H. H.
abstract: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) was used to image and measure the passive sound-driven displacements of cochlear structures in situ through the intact round window membrane of fresh human cadaveric specimens at 12 to 30 hours postmortem. We find that the anatomical integrity of the organ of Corti (OoC) affects cochlear structural motion. OoC with high integrity (erect with supporting cells) have small osseous spiral lamina (OSL) motion. Conversely, OoC with low integrity (flattened without supporting cells) have large OSL motion. For the ratio of motion between the basilar membrane (BM) and OSL (BM/OSL), OoC with high integrity has large BM/OSL motion while a cochlear partition without OoC has small BM/OSL motion. Furthermore, the high-integrity OoC has reticular lamina surface motion that is lower than the BM, whereas low-integrity OoC has similar reticular lamina and BM motion. This relationship between OoC anatomical integrity and cochlear structural motion will have consequential effects on sound transduction.

title: Modelling prodromal Parkinson's disease- gastrointestinal pathology and early motor deficits in mice after transient rotenone exposure
authors: Selvaraji, S.; Mosberger, J.; Pang, K. K. L.; Eberly, G. L.; Kim, Y. J.; Mondal, R.; Leomi, R.; Anikeeva, P.
abstract: Early gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is a hallmark feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet models capturing prodromal gut and brain pathology in PD remain limited. Motivated by the increased PD risk associated with pesticide exposure, we monitored motor behavior, brain pathology, and GI structure and function over 9 months following 5 daily doses of rotenone in mice. Transient rotenone exposure induced significant nigrostriatal pathology, including {approx}48% loss of dopaminergic neurons and increased -synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra, without significant changes in gross motor function. Notably, we identified pronounced GI dysfunction including reduced colonic transit velocity, altered motility dynamics, and delayed whole-gut transit. These functional changes were accompanied by enteric dopaminergic neurodegeneration, increased colonic -synuclein accumulation, increased colonic crypt depth, goblet cell hyperplasia with elevated mucin content per goblet cell. The findings are consistent with prodromal PD, suggesting the utility of this model for investigating early disease mechanisms and intervention strategies.

title: Alzheimer's Disease-Associated Proteomic Changes in Olfactory Stem Cells Show Pathway-Level Transcriptomic Overlap
authors: Rantanen, L. M.; Robinson, H.; DutraVoigt, D.; Diaz, X.; Lampinen, R.; Mykkanen, S.; Kalapudas, J.; Koivisto, A. M.; Penttila, E.; Oikari, L. E.; Quek, H.; Kanninen, K. M.; White, A. R.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive, neurodegenerative disorder and the leading cause of dementia worldwide. Although recent therapeutic advances have provided some disease-modifying potential, there is currently no curative treatment for AD, highlighting the need for improved disease models and early biomarkers. Olfactory mucosal stem cells, which can be expanded in vitro as olfactory neurosphere-derived (ONS) cells, represent a promising source for biomarker discovery because olfactory tissue is more accessible than central nervous system tissue and has been reported to exhibit AD-related pathological changes. In this study, we used subcellular fractionation-based proteomics, reconstructed bulk proteomics and integrated transcriptomic-proteomic analyses to characterise alterations in ONS cells derived from healthy control, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD individuals. Fraction-specific proteomics identified cytoplasmic and nuclear-enriched protein abundance changes, including alterations in proteins and pathways associated with cytoskeletal organisation, RNA processing, intracellular trafficking, autophagy and mitochondrial/metabolic processes. Reduced LC3B abundance in cytoplasmic AD ONS cells was supported by western blot analysis, although LC3B abundance alone does not indicate altered autophagic flux. Reconstructed bulk proteomics identified 40 FDR-significant proteins in AD compared with HC, defining an AD-associated protein signature enriched for extracellular matrix, cytoskeletal, organelle-associated and RNA-processing pathways. Despite proteomic enrichment of mitochondrial and metabolic pathways, Seahorse Mito Stress Test analysis did not identify significant group-level differences in mitochondrial respiration. Integrated transcriptomic-proteomic analysis revealed partial RNA-protein concordance and pathway-level overlap across disease-associated processes. Together, these findings support the use of patient-derived ONS cells as a model for investigating AD- and MCI-associated molecular changes and highlight protein signatures for further validation.
